exercises.objective: Derive PCA's optimal mu and z_i from the projection-error minimization objective.
exercises.prompt: For fixed $V_p$, minimize $\sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i-(V_pz_i+\mu)\|^2$ over $\mu$ and $z_{1:n}$ by setting the relevant partial derivatives to zero. Show $\hat z_i=V_p^\top(x_i-\mu)$ for each $i$, assuming $V_p^\top V_p=I$ (orthonormal columns).
hints: Differentiate w.r.t. $z_i$ (each $z_i$ only appears in the $i$-th term of the sum): $\frac{\partial}{\partial z_i}\|x_i-V_pz_i-\mu\|^2 = -2V_p^\top(x_i-V_pz_i-\mu)$.
Setting this to zero: $V_p^\top(x_i-\mu) = V_p^\top V_pz_i$. Using $V_p^\top V_p=I$ (orthonormal columns), this simplifies directly.

$\hat z_i = V_p^\top(x_i-\mu)$: the optimal latent code is just the orthogonal projection of the centered point onto $V_p$'s columns. (Differentiating w.r.t. $\mu$ similarly, summing over $i$ and setting to zero, gives $\hat\mu=\langle x_i\rangle$, the data mean, using that $\sum_i\hat z_i$-related terms cancel once $\mu$ is the mean.)

exercises.objective: Explain the kernel PCA idea as an application of ML-05's kernel trick.
exercises.prompt: Explain what specifically has to be true about PCA's computation for it to be kernelizable the same way ridge regression was, and what capability kernel PCA gains as a result.
hints: PCA's computation (finding eigenvectors of $X^\top X=\sum_i\tilde x_i\tilde x_i^\top$) only ever needs inner products between (centered) data points, never the raw coordinates individually, exactly the condition ML-05 identified as kernelizable.

So replacing every inner product $\tilde x_i^\top\tilde x_j$ with a kernel evaluation $k(x_i,x_j)$ gives 'kernel PCA': the eigendecomposition is now performed on the kernel (Gram) matrix $K$ instead of $X^\top X$ directly.

The gain: kernel PCA implicitly operates in the kernel's (possibly infinite-dimensional, non-linear) feature space, so it can uncover structure (e.g. separating clusters) that no *linear* projection of the raw data ever could, exactly the same expressive gain the kernel trick gave ridge regression.

exercises.objective: Run one iteration of k-means by hand on a small dataset and compute a new cluster center.
exercises.prompt: Data points $(1,1),(1,2),(8,8),(9,9)$; initial centers $\mu_1=(0,0),\mu_2=(10,10)$. After one assignment step (each point to its nearest center) and one re-centering step, what is the $y$-coordinate of the new $\mu_1$? Enter a decimal.
hints: Compute each point's distance to $\mu_1=(0,0)$ and $\mu_2=(10,10)$: $(1,1)$ and $(1,2)$ are clearly much closer to $(0,0)$; $(8,8)$ and $(9,9)$ are clearly much closer to $(10,10)$.
New $\mu_1$ = mean of $(1,1)$ and $(1,2)$ = $(1,\,1.5)$. The $y$-coordinate is $1.5$. (Independently verified with NumPy while authoring this module; new $\mu_2=(8.5,8.5)$ for reference.)

exercises.objective: Explain how k-means arises as a limiting case of GMM/EM.
exercises.prompt: Explain what happens to the GMM E-step's soft assignment $q(c_i{=}k)$ as every cluster's covariance $\Sigma_k\to0$ (with equal, small, isotropic covariances), and why that recovers k-means's hard assignment.
hints: $q(c_i{=}k)\propto\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\pi_k$; as $\Sigma_k\to0$ (shrinking, equal across clusters), the Gaussian density becomes extremely sharply peaked around $\mu_k$.

For a given $x_i$, whichever $\mu_k$ is nearest will have overwhelmingly larger density than any other $\mu_{k'}$ once the covariance is small enough, since the Gaussian density falls off so fast away from its mean.

So $q(c_i{=}k)\to1$ for the nearest center and $\to0$ for every other, exactly k-means's hard assignment $c(i)=\operatorname*{argmin}_k\|x_i-\mu_k\|^2$; the M-step's mean update also matches k-means's re-centering step in this limit, since the soft weights collapse to 0/1 indicators.
